newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION -From the Beehive, Peters the monetarist?.
newsitem.headline: OPINION -From the Beehive, Peters the monetarist?.

text.p: WELLINGTON, DEC 23 - It was just as if Bill Birch was speaking , a senior National cabinet minister remarked, wonderingly, after Winston Peters delivered his first fiscal presentation to Cabinet last week.
Peters talked of the need to cut the fat out of state spending, and warned spending ministers that he was going to be just as ruthless as his two predecessors.

So is this just another somersault from the Winston Peters the country got to know in the run-up to the election, the political leader who promised big new spending programmes in employment, education and health.
Or is New Zealand watching the transmutation of NZ First s leader from a political dazzler into a fiscal heavyweight?
The jury might be out for some months yet.
But the evidence is that those who talked up the prospect of a retreat into Muldoonism with the elevation of Peters into the role of Treasurer might have mis-read the book.
Peters tells anyone who will listen that he plans to be the most fiscally responsible minister of the modern era.
That has already led to accusations that he has been nobbled by Treasury.
The truth is rather different, as those Treasury officials who have been on the receiving end of terse responses from Peters, or his associate John Delamere, will testify.
Peters took no prisoners in his turf wars with Birch over their respective responsibilities as Treasurer, and Minister of Finance.

Those wars were as intense as any in the coalition negotiations, and when Prime Minister Jim Bolger told them last week, when the issue was still unresolved: "You two sort it out between...because you ve got to work together."

It appears that NZ First s eminence gris Wayne Peters had to be called in to assist with drafting the protocols aimed at the guidance of officials and staff. What restricted Peters from a full takeover was the requirement that the National caucus has to be briefed on all financial matters; only Birch can do that, and so he has to have access to all Treasury papers.
And as was apparent at the first cabinet meeting, Birch carries in his head his own database on the financial structure of New Zealand's state sector.
He was the minister who had the answers when some of the new ministers in charge of spending departments started throwing questions at the Treasurer.

Birch will be involved, in conjunction with the Treasurer, in the programme of scrutinising baseline and new policy budget bids, and as the minister responsible for expenditure, he has the power to approve, or knock back, new policy bids.

In that light, the new arrangement, even if it has inbuilt tensions, should enable a tight hold to be maintained on government expenditure. Arguably, then, what has happened is rather different from what some commentators have pictured.

The Economist, for example, contended that the government will be one of fudge and mudge for the next three years; while Gareth Morgan of Infometrics says that Muldoonism is back, firmly in control and those who brought us Think Big, arguably the raison d'etre for 12 years of economic principles they started with.

But if it's true that Peters has dropped the populism that won him the role of power broker in favour of being the fundementalist Tory he has always been, then he may surprise those who fear that the era of fiscal surpluses, low inflation, tax cuts and declining public debt has ended prematurely.
(Note - The opinions expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters)
